entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.1">Lev 13:1</reference> <div eID="gen1308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1309" type="x-p"/> Leprosy. - The law for leprosy, the observance of which is urged upon the people again in <reference osisRef="Deut.24.8-Deut.24.9">Deu 24:8-9</reference>, treats, in the <hi type="italic">first</hi> place, of leprosy in men: (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) in its dangerous forms when appearing either on the skin (vv. 2-28), or on the head and beard (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.29-Lev.13.37">Lev 13:29-37</reference>); (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) in harmless forms (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.38">Lev 13:38</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.13.39">Lev 13:39</reference>); and (<hi type="italic">c</hi>) when appearing on a bald head (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.40-Lev.13.44">Lev 13:40-44</reference>). To this there are added instructions for the removal of the leper from the society of other men (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.45">Lev 13:45</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.13.46">Lev 13:46</reference>). It treats, <hi type="italic">secondly</hi>, of leprosy in linen, woollen, and leather articles, and the way to treat them (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.47-Lev.13.59">Lev 13:47-59</reference>); <hi type="italic">thirdly</hi>, of the purification of persons recovered from leprosy (<reference osisRef="Lev.14.1-Lev.14.32">Lev 14:1-32</reference>); and <hi type="italic">fourthly</hi>, of leprosy in houses and the way to remove it (vv. 33-53). - The laws for leprosy in man relate exclusively to the so-called white leprosy, λεύκη λέπρα, <hi type="italic">lepra</hi>, which probably existed at that time in hither Asia alone, not only among the Israelites and Jews (Num 12:10.; <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.29">2Sa 3:29</reference>; 2Ki 5:27; 2Ki 7:3; 2Ki 15:5; <reference osisRef="Matt.8.2-Matt.8.3">Mat 8:2-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.8">Mat 10:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.5">Mat 11:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.6">Mat 26:6</reference>, etc.), but also among the Syrians (2Ki 5:1.), and which is still found in that part of the world, most frequently in the countries of the Lebanon and Jordan and in the neighbourhood of Damascus, in which city there are three hospitals for lepers (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, pp. 277, 278), and occasionally in Arabia (<hi type="italic">Niebuhr, Arab.</hi> pp. 135ff.) and Egypt; though at the present time the pimply leprosy, <hi type="italic">lepra tuberosa s. articulorum</hi> (the leprosy of the joints), is more prevalent in the East, and frequently occurs in Egypt in the lower extremities in the form of elephantiasis. Of the white leprosy (called <hi type="italic">Lepra Mosaica</hi>), which is still met with in Arabia sometimes, where it is called <hi type="italic">Baras</hi>, <hi type="italic">Trusen</hi> gives the following description: “Very frequently, even for years before the actual outbreak of the disease itself, white, yellowish spots are seen lying deep in the skin, particularly on the genitals, in the face, on the forehead, or in the joints. They are without feeling, and sometimes cause the hair to assume the same colour as the spots. These spots afterwards pierce through the cellular tissue, and reach the muscles and bones. The hair becomes white and woolly, and at length falls off; hard gelatinous swellings are formed in the cellular tissue; the skin gets hard, rough, and seamy, lymph exudes from it, and forms large scabs, which fall off from time to time, and under these there are often offensive running sores. The nails then swell, curl up, and fall off; <hi type="italic">entropium</hi> is formed, with bleeding gums, the nose stopped up, and a considerable flow of saliva... The senses become dull, the patient gets thin and weak, colliquative diarrhea sets in, and incessant thirst and burning fever terminate his sufferings” (<hi type="italic">Krankheiten d. alten Hebr. </hi>p. 165).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.2-Lev.13.28">Lev 13:2-28</reference> <hi type="italic">The symptoms of leprosy, whether proceeding directly from eruptions in the skin, or caused by a boil or burn</hi>. - <reference osisRef="Lev.13.2">Lev 13:2</reference>-8. <hi type="italic">The first case:</hi> “When a man shall have in the skin of his flesh (body) a raised spot or scab, or a bright spot.” שׂאת, a lifting up (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.7">Gen 4:7</reference>, etc.), signifies here an elevation of the skin in some part of the body, a raised spot like a pimple. ספּחת, an eruption, scurf, or scab, from ספח to pour out, “a pouring out as it were from the flesh or skin” (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>). בּהרת .)le, from בּהר, in the Arabic and Chaldee to shine, is a bright swollen spot in the skin. If ether of these signs became “a spot of leprosy,” the person affected was to be brought to the priest, that he might examine the complaint. The term <hi type="italic">zaraath</hi>, from an Arabic word signifying to strike down or scourge, is applied to leprosy as a scourge of God, and in the case of men it always denotes the white leprosy, which the Arabs call <hi type="italic">baras</hi>. נגע, a stroke (lit., “stroke of leprosy”), is applied not only to the spot attacked by the leprosy, the leprous mole (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.3">Lev 13:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.29-Lev.13.32">Lev 13:29-32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.42">Lev 13:42</reference>, etc.), but to the persons and even to things affected with leprosy (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.4">Lev 13:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.12">Lev 13:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.13">Lev 13:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.31">Lev 13:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.50">Lev 13:50</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.55">Lev 13:55</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.29-Lev.13.31">Lev 13:29-31</reference> <hi type="italic">Leprosy upon the head or chin</hi>. - If the priest saw a mole upon the head or chin of a man or woman, the appearance of which was deeper than the skin, and on which the hair was yellow (צהב golden, reddish, fox-colour) and thin, he was to regard it as נתק. Leprosy on the head or chin is called נתק, probably from נתק to pluck or tear, from its plucking out the hair, or causing it to fall off; like κνήφη, the itch, from κνάω, to itch or scratch, and <hi type="italic">scabies</hi>, from <hi type="italic">scabere</hi>. But if he did not observe these two symptoms, if there was no depression of the skin, and the hair was black and not yellow, he was to shut up the person affected for seven days. In בּו אין שׁחר (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.31">Lev 13:31</reference>) there is certainly an error of the text: either שׁחר must be retained and אין dropped, or שׁהר must be altered into צהב, according to Lev 13:37. The latter is probably the better of the two.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.32-Lev.13.34">Lev 13:32-34</reference> <div eID="gen1318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1319" type="x-p"/> If the mole had not spread by that time, and the two signs mentioned were not discernible, the person affected was to shave himself, but not to shave the nethek, the eruption or scurfy place, and the priest was to shut him up for seven days more, and then to look whether any alteration had taken place; and if not, to pronounce him clean, whereupon he was to wash his clothes (see <reference osisRef="Lev.13.6">Lev 13:6</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.35-Lev.13.36">Lev 13:35-36</reference> <div eID="gen1319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1320" type="x-p"/> But if the eruption spread even after his purification, the priest, on seeing this, was not to look for yellow hair. “He is unclean:” that is to say, he was to pronounce him unclean without searching for yellow hairs; the spread of the eruption was a sufficient proof of the leprosy.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.38-Lev.13.39">Lev 13:38-39</reference> <hi type="italic">Harmless leprosy</hi>. - This broke out upon the skin of the body in בּהרת plaits, “white rings.” If these were dull or a pale white, it was the harmless <hi type="italic">bohak</hi>, ἀλφός (lxx), which did not defile, and which even the Arabs, who still call it <hi type="italic">bahak</hi>, consider harmless. It is an eruption upon the skin, appearing in somewhat elevated spots or rings of inequal sizes and a pale white colour, which do not change the hair; it causes no inconvenience, and lasts from two months to two years.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.40-Lev.13.41">Lev 13:40-41</reference> <hi type="italic">The leprosy of bald heads</hi>. - קרח is a head bald behind; גּבּח, in front, “bald from the side, or edge of his face, i.e., from the forehead and temples.” Bald heads of both kinds were naturally clean.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.45-Lev.13.46">Lev 13:45-46</reference> <div eID="gen1322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1323" type="x-p"/> With regard to <hi type="italic">the treatment of lepers</hi>, the lawgiver prescribed that they should wear mourning costume, rend their clothes, leave the hair of their head in disorder (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.10.6">Lev 10:6</reference>), keep the beard covered (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.17">Eze 24:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.22">Eze 24:22</reference>), and cry “Unclean, unclean,” that every one might avoid them for fear of being defiled (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.15">Lam 4:15</reference>); and as long as the disease lasted they were to dwell apart outside the camp (Num 5:2., Num 12:10., cf. 2Ki 15:5; 2Ki 7:3),<note placement="foot">At the present day there are pest-houses specially set apart for lepers outside the towns. In Jerusalem they are situated against the Zion-gate (see Robinson, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> i.p. 364).</note> a rule which implies that the leper rendered others unclean by contact. From this the Rabbins taught, that by merely entering a house, a leper polluted everything within it (<hi type="italic">Mishnah</hi>, Kelim i. 4; Negaim xiii. 11).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.47-Lev.13.52">Lev 13:47-52</reference> <hi type="italic">Leprosy in linen, woollen, and leather fabrics and clothes</hi>. - The only wearing apparel mentioned in <reference osisRef="Lev.13.47">Lev 13:47</reference> is either woollen or linen, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.22.11">Deu 22:11</reference>; Hos 2:7; <reference osisRef="Prov.31.13">Pro 31:13</reference>; and among the ancient Egyptians and ancient Greeks these were the materials usually worn. In Lev 13:48. שׁתי and ערב, “the flax and the wool,” i.e., for linen and woollen fabrics, are distinguished from clothes of wool or flax. The rendering given to these words by the early translators is στήμων and κρόκη, <hi type="italic">stamen et subtegmen</hi> (lxx, Vulg.), i.e., warp and weft. The objection offered to this rendering, that warp and weft could not be kept so separate from one another, that the one could be touched and rendered leprous without the other, has been met by <hi type="italic">Gussetius</hi> by the simple but correct remark, that the reference is to the yarn prepared for the warp and weft, and not to the woven fabrics themselves. So long as the yarn was not woven into a fabric, the warp-yarn and weft-yarn might very easily be separated and lie in different places, so that the one could be injured without the other. In this case the yarn intended for weaving is distinguished from the woven material, just as the leather is afterwards distinguished from leather-work (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.49">Lev 13:49</reference>). The signs of leprosy were, if the mole in the fabric was greenish or reddish. In that case the priest was to shut up the thing affected with leprosy for seven days, and then examine it. If the mole had spread in the meantime, it was a “grievous leprosy.” ממארת, from מאר <hi type="italic">irritavit, recruduit</hi> (<hi type="italic">vulnus</hi>), is to be explained, as it is by <hi type="italic">Bochart</hi>, as signifying <hi type="italic">lepra exasperata</hi>. הנּגע ממארת making the mole bad or angry; not, as <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> maintains, from מאר = מרר <hi type="italic">acerbum faciens</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">dolorem acerbum excitans</hi>, which would not apply to leprosy in fabrics and houses (<reference osisRef="Lev.14.44">Lev 14:44</reference>), and is not required by Eze 28:24. All such fabrics were to be burned as unclean.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.53-Lev.13.55">Lev 13:53-55</reference> <div eID="gen1323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1324" type="x-p"/> If the mole had not spread during the seven days, the priest was to cause the fabric in which the mole appeared to be washed, and then shut it up for seven days more. If the mole did not alter its appearance after being washed, even though it had not spread, the fabric was unclean, and was therefore to be burned. “It is a corroding in the back and front” (of the fabric of leather). פּחתת, from פּחת, in Syriac <hi type="italic">fodit</hi>, from which comes פּחת a pit, lit., a digging: here a corroding depression. קרחת a bald place in the front or right side, גּבּחת a bald place in the back or left side of the fabric or leather.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.56">Lev 13:56</reference> <div eID="gen1324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1325" type="x-p"/> But if the mole had turned pale by the seventh day after the washing, it (the place of the mole) was to be separated (torn off) from the clothes, leather or yarn, and then (as is added afterwards in <reference osisRef="Lev.13.58">Lev 13:58</reference>) the garment or fabric from which the mole had disappeared was to be washed a second time, and would then be clean.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.57-Lev.13.59">Lev 13:57-59</reference> <div eID="gen1325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1326" type="x-p"/> But if the mole appeared <hi type="italic">again</hi> in any such garment or cloth, i.e., if it appeared again after this, it was a leprosy bursting forth afresh, and the thing affected with it was to be burned. Leprosy in linen and woollen fabrics or clothes, and in leather, consisted in all probability in nothing but so-called mildew, which commonly arises from damp and want of air, and consists, in the case of linen, of round, partially coloured spots, which spread, and gradually eat up the fabric, until it falls to pieces like mould. In leather the mildew consists most strictly of “holes eaten in,” and is of a “greenish, reddish, or whitish colour, according to the species of the delicate cryptogami by which it has been formed.”  <chapter eID="Lev.13"/> <div eID="gen1326" type="x-p"/>
